title: Cheque Bouncing under NI Act s.138 (Pakistan)
query: What is the procedure and punishment for cheque bouncing under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act in Pakistan?
memo:
# LEGAL MEMORANDUM: CHEQUE DISHONOUR PROCEDURE & PUNISHMENT UNDER PAKISTANI LAW

---

## PREMISE CORRECTION

**Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act (India) does not apply in Pakistan.** The criminal offence of cheque dishonour under Section 138 NI Act 1881 is an Indian statutory provision (inserted by Act 66 of 1988) and does not exist in the Pakistan Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. In the Pakistan NI Act 1881, Section 138 merely provides for the appointment of Notaries Public and bears no relation to criminal prosecution for dishonour.

**In Pakistan, criminal prosecution for dishonour of a cheque is governed exclusively by Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, 1860** (inserted by Criminal Law (Amendment) Ordinance, 2002 [LXXXV of 2002]), and summary civil recovery may be pursued under Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

---

## Legal Issue

What is the procedure for criminal prosecution and the applicable punishment for dishonestly issuing a cheque that is dishonoured on presentation under Pakistani law, and what statutory defences are available to the accused?

---

## Relevant Provisions

### 1. Section 489-F, Pakistan Penal Code, 1860

**Status**: In Force (as amended by Criminal Law [Amendment] Ordinance, 2002)

**Verbatim Text**:

> "Whoever dishonestly issues a cheque towards re-payment of a loan or fulfilment of an obligation which is dishonoured on presentation, shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, unless he can establish, that he had made arrangements with his bank to ensure that the cheque would be honoured and that the bank was at fault in not honouring the cheque."

**Key Elements**:
- The offence is **cognizable** (police may arrest without warrant).
- The offence is **non-bailable** under Schedule II of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1898.
- The offence is **compoundable** (parties may settle).
- Trial forum: **Magistrate of the First Class**.
- Punishment: Imprisonment (up to 3 years) or fine, or both.

### 2. Section 118, Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881

**Status**: In Force

**Verbatim Text**:

> "Presumptions as to negotiable instruments. Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made: (a) of consideration; that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration… (g) that holder is a holder in due course: provided that, where the instrument has been obtained from its lawful owner, or from any person in lawful custody thereof, by means of an offence or fraud, or has been obtained from the maker or acceptor thereof by means of an offence or fraud, or for unlawful consideration, the burthen of proving that the holder is a holder in due course lies upon him."

**Applicability**: These statutory presumptions apply to cheques presented as evidence in proceedings under Section 489-F.

### 3. Order XXXVII, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

**Status**: In Force (Summary procedure on negotiable instruments)

Statutory text not found in verified database.

---

## Judicial Authorities

### 1. Muhammad Tariq Javed v. State — 2008 YLR 947

- **Court**: Lahore High Court
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority (Section 489-F PPC, same statutory framework)
- **Relevant facts**: The petitioner had admitted issuance of a cheque for payment of an obligation. The cheque was presented after 40 days and was dishonoured. The complainant was twice deprived of the hard-earned money.
- **Court held**: Where issuance of a cheque is admitted by the accused and the cheque is dishonoured, the offence under Section 489-F PPC is **fully attracted**.
- **Ratio decidendi**: Admission of cheque issuance coupled with dishonour constitutes the complete factual foundation for the Section 489-F offence; no further evidentiary hurdle arises at the stage of bail consideration when the criminal ingredients are demonstrable.

### 2. Shahid Aziz v. State — 2007 YLR 1810

- **Court**: Lahore High Court
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority (Section 489-F PPC, same statutory framework)
- **Relevant facts**: An FIR was lodged with a delay of one month. The petitioner denied signing the cheque. A Forensic Science Lab report confirmed that the petitioner had not signed the cheque. The Bank Manager also supported the petitioner's stand. The complainant and petitioner had a business dispute.
- **Court held**: For Section 489-F to apply, it is a **condition precedent** that the cheque was given by the accused for "repayment of a loan or fulfilment of an obligation." A mere business dispute does not satisfy this statutory condition. Where the accused's signature on the cheque is denied and forensic evidence supports that denial, the foundational element of the offence is absent.
- **Ratio decidendi**: The statutory language of Section 489-F PPC imposes an essential precondition: the cheque must have been issued specifically towards repayment of a loan or fulfilment of an obligation. Mere commercial or business disputes fall outside this definition. Forensic evidence negating the accused's authorship of the cheque eliminates the offence entirely.

### 3. Zulfiqar Haider v. State — 2006 YLR 961

- **Court**: Lahore High Court
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority (Section 489-F PPC, same statutory framework)
- **Relevant facts**: A cheque was allegedly issued on 13-1-2005 but presented for encashment on 20-6-2004 (temporally impossible). The cheque had been altered (figure '2' converted to '4'). The cheque was not included in the FIR. Critically, the cheque was initially issued on 13-1-2002, before Section 489-F was enacted on 25-10-2002.
- **Court held**: Where a cheque was issued before Section 489-F came into force, the criminal offence cannot be attracted retroactively. Additionally, unexplained alterations to the cheque and temporal impossibilities (presentation before issuance) cast serious doubt on the prosecution case and require further inquiry.
- **Ratio decidendi**: Section 489-F PPC has prospective operation only; cheques dishonoured prior to 25-10-2002 cannot be prosecuted under this section. Alterations to cheques and temporal inconsistencies are material to the veracity of the cheque as a negotiable instrument and must be investigated by the trial court.

### 4. Hakeem v. State — 2026 SCMR 792

- **Court**: Supreme Court of Pakistan
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority (Section 489-F PPC, same statutory framework and appellate forum)
- **Relevant facts**: The accused was charged with offences under Sections 420, 406, 489-F PPC (and Section 34 PPC for common intention). The question arose whether Section 489-F offences fell within the non-prohibitory clause of Section 497 Criminal Procedure Code (relating to bail).
- **Court held**: Section 489-F offences fall within the **non-prohibitory clause of Section 497 Cr.P.C.**, meaning that bail is the rule and refusal is the exception. Courts must consider the grant of bail favourably where offences fall within the non-prohibitory category. Bail may be refused only in **exceptional circumstances**, including: (i) likelihood of abscondence; (ii) apprehension of tampering with prosecution evidence; or (iii) danger of repetition of the offence.
- **Ratio decidendi**: Offences under Section 489-F PPC are non-prohibitory under Section 497 Cr.P.C., reversing the legal presumption in favour of the accused. The prosecution and complainant bear the burden of demonstrating exceptional circumstances to justify pre-arrest or post-arrest bail refusal.

### 5. Aqeel Ahmed Khan v. State — 2025 SCMR 1955

- **Court**: Supreme Court of Pakistan
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority (Section 489-F PPC, same statutory framework and appellate forum)
- **Relevant facts**: The petitioner was charged with an offence under Section 489-F PPC. The legal question concerned whether this offence fell within the non-prohibitory clause of Section 497 Cr.P.C.
- **The judgment record indicates**: Section 489-F offences are admittedly of the category that falls within the non-prohibitory clause of Section 497 Cr.P.C., confirming that bail is ordinarily to be granted as a rule in these matters.
- **Ratio decidendi**: Consistent with *Hakeem v. State*, the Supreme Court has reaffirmed that Section 489-F offences are non-bailable in the sense that they do not trigger an absolute prohibition on bail under the prohibitory clauses of Section 497 Cr.P.C.; rather, they fall within the discretionary category where bail may be granted or refused on case-specific grounds.

---

## Application to Query

### Procedure for Criminal Prosecution under Section 489-F PPC

The criminal procedure for prosecuting cheque dishonour in Pakistan is as follows:

title: Banking Court Auction under FIO 2001
query: Can a banking court execute a decree by auctioning mortgaged property without fresh proclamation under FIO 2001?
memo:
# Legal Memorandum: Execution of Decree by Auctioning Mortgaged Property Without Fresh Proclamation Under FIO 2001

## Legal Issue

Whether a Banking Court executing a decree under the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001 (FIO 2001) may proceed directly to auction mortgaged property without issuing a fresh proclamation of sale, or whether the statutory scheme mandates specific procedural steps before conducting such auction.

## Relevant Provisions

> Statutory text unavailable in retrieved sources. The analysis is based only on judicial references.

The retrieved authorities reference:
- **Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001** — Section 19 (Automatic conversion of suit into execution and execution procedures)
- **Civil Procedure Code, 1908** — Order XXI, Rule 90 (Objection petitions to auction proceedings)

## Judicial Authorities

### The BANK OF PUNJAB VS AGRI INTERNATIONAL — 2026 CLD 432
- **Court**: Lahore High Court
- **Authority Level**: Analogical Authority (Decisions on FIO 2001 execution are analogous to the statutory framework; however, this judgment does not directly address the requirement of fresh proclamation before auction)
- **Relevant facts**: Banking Court executed a judgment and decree by conducting an auction of mortgaged property.
- **Court held**: Auction is subject to conditions and a conscious order passed in this respect under Section 19(1) read with Section 19(3) of the Ordinance, 2001. Section 19(1) provides for automatic conversion of suit into execution, with an exception to the requirement of instituting a separate execution application and issuing notices to judgment debtor.
- **Ratio decidendi**: Under FIO 2001, Section 19(1), the Banking Court has authority to conduct auction proceedings as part of automatic conversion of suit into execution, provided that a conscious and reasoned order is passed under Section 19(1) read with Section 19(3). The statutory scheme contemplates auction as a mode of execution within the Banking Court's inherent authority.

### NOOR HAYAT COTTON GINNERS VS The BANK OF PUNJAB — 2026 CLD 68
- **Court**: Lahore High Court
- **Authority Level**: Analogical Authority (Decisions on FIO 2001 execution procedures; however, this judgment addresses objection petitions to auction, not the antecedent question of proclamation)
- **Relevant facts**: In order to execute the judgment and decree passed by the Banking Court, an auction was conducted for the sale of mortgaged property. An Objection Petition was filed under Order XXI, Rule 90 C.P.C. against the auction proceedings.
- **Court held**: The condition to deposit 50% of the sale proceeds under Order XXI, Rule 90 C.P.C. is mandatory when the Executing Court specifically requires such deposit and warns of consequences of non-deposit. Where appellants failed to make the required deposit, the Objection Petition was dismissed with no illegality, infirmity, or jurisdictional defect.
- **Ratio decidendi**: Objection petitions challenging auction proceedings are subject to procedural conditions (deposit requirement) imposed by the Executing Court. Failure to comply with these conditions results in dismissal. The judgment record does not indicate that a fresh proclamation is a mandatory pre-condition to auction.

## Application to Query

Based on the judicial authorities retrieved, the following observations emerge:

1. **Automatic Conversion and Auction Authority**: The judgment record indicates (2026 CLD 432) that Section 19(1) of FIO 2001 provides for automatic conversion of suit into execution. The Court held that auction is subject to conditions and a conscious order passed under Section 19(1) read with Section 19(3). The statutory scheme appears to contemplate that the Banking Court may proceed to auction as part of the execution process.

2. **Absence of Fresh Proclamation Requirement**: The retrieved authorities do not establish that a fresh proclamation of sale is a mandatory prerequisite to auction under FIO 2001. The judgment record indicates (2026 CLD 68) that auction proceedings were conducted in order to execute the judgment and decree passed by the Banking Court, with objection petitions being filed thereafter under the procedural framework of Order XXI, Rule 90 C.P.C. Neither judgment articulates a requirement for fresh proclamation prior to auction.

3. **Procedural Safeguards in Execution**: While the authorities confirm that auction must be conducted subject to a conscious order of the Court and procedural conditions (such as deposit requirements for objection petitions), they do not indicate that the absence of a fresh proclamation renders the auction void or unauthorised.

**An inference from the cited authorities is** that under FIO 2001, the Banking Court may execute a decree by auctioning mortgaged property in reliance upon Section 19(1)'s automatic conversion mechanism, provided that a reasoned order is passed. However, the precise scope of the proclamation requirement—whether it must be fresh or may rely on prior proclamation—is not directly decided by the retrieved judgments.

The issue depends on the complete statutory text of Section 19 FIO 2001, which was not retrieved in the present sources. Accordingly, reliance on judicial observation alone indicates that procedural safeguards and conscious ordering are required, but does not definitively resolve whether a fresh proclamation is mandatory before auction proceeds.

title: Orphaned Grandchild Inheritance under MFLO Section 4
query: Does an orphaned grandchild have a right to inherit from their grandfather's estate under Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961?
memo:
# LEGAL MEMORANDUM: INHERITANCE RIGHTS OF ORPHANED GRANDCHILD UNDER MUSLIM FAMILY LAWS ORDINANCE 1961

## Legal Issue
Whether an orphaned grandchild (whose father or mother has predeceased) possesses a right to inherit from their grandfather's estate under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961.

## Relevant Provisions

> Statutory text unavailable in retrieved sources. The analysis is based only on judicial references.

The Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 governs succession and inheritance matters for Muslims in Pakistan. The retrieved judicial authorities reference the Ordinance but the complete statutory text on succession and the specific status of orphaned grandchildren in inheritance has not been retrieved in the primary sources consulted.

## Judicial Authorities

### Analysis of Retrieved Precedents

The five Supreme Court precedents supplied (2026 SCMR 1, PLD 2025 SC 469, PLD 2026 SC 20, PLD 2026 SC 302, PLD 2026 SC 91) address matters of:
- Maintenance entitlements under Section 9, MFLO (2026 SCMR 1)
- Finality of divorce and widow's inheritance rights under Section 7(3), MFLO (PLD 2025 SC 469)
- Form and registration of marriage contracts under Section 5, MFLO (PLD 2026 SC 20)
- Dissolution of marriage upon husband's second marriage under Sections 6 & 8, MFLO (PLD 2026 SC 302 and PLD 2026 SC 91)
- Statutory grounds for dissolution of marriage (PLD 2026 SC 91)

**Critical Limitation on Authority Relevance:**

None of the retrieved Supreme Court precedents directly address:
- The succession status of orphaned grandchildren
- The line of descent or inheritance hierarchy under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961
- The conditions under which a grandchild, whose parent has predeceased, acquires inheritance rights
- The interaction between Islamic law of succession (as applied under MFLO) and the concept of representation or *per stirpes* inheritance

The retrieved authorities are classified as **Analogical Authority** (addressing family law matters under MFLO but not the specific succession question at issue). They do not provide controlling precedent on the exact legal issue posed.

## Application to Query

**I did not find a case that squarely holds a specific principle regarding the inheritance rights of orphaned grandchildren under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961.**

The Supreme Court decisions retrieved address dissolution of marriage, maintenance entitlements, and marriage registration—matters distinct from the succession rights of grandchildren. While PLD 2025 SC 469 discusses a widow's entitlement to inherit her deceased husband's estate, it does not address the succession status of lineal descendants beyond the immediate heirs, nor does it clarify whether an orphaned grandchild (whose parent has predeceased) succeeds to their grandparent's estate.

To properly answer this query, direct authority addressing:
- Section(s) of MFLO governing succession and inheritance order
- Judicial application of Islamic law principles on representation (*per stirpes*) or inheritance by grandchildren when their parent is deceased
- Supreme Court or High Court precedent squarely deciding the inheritance rights of orphaned grandchildren

would be required. No such authority has been retrieved.

title: Auction Challenge Limitation under Order XXI Rule 90 CPC
query: What is the limitation period for challenging an auction sale under Order XXI Rule 90 CPC?
memo:
# LEGAL MEMORANDUM — LIMITATION PERIOD FOR CHALLENGING AUCTION SALE UNDER ORDER XXI RULE 90 CPC

## Legal Issue
What is the statutory or judicially established limitation period within which an application to set aside an auction sale under Order XXI Rule 90 CPC must be filed?

## Relevant Provisions

**Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 — Order XXI Rule 90:**
"90. Application to set aside sale on ground of irregularity or fraud.__ (1) Where any immoveable property has been sold in execution of a decree, the decree-holder, or any person entitled to share in a rateable distribution of assets, or whose interests are affected by the sale, may apply to the Court to set aside the sale on the ground of a material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting it:
Provided that no sale shall be set aside on the ground of irregularity or fraud unless upon the facts proved the Court is satisfied that the applicant has sustained substantial injury by reason of such irregularity or fraud:
Provided further that no such application shall be entertained unless the applicant deposits such amount, not exceeding twenty per cent of the sum realised at the sale, or furnishes such security, as the Court may direct."

---

## Judicial Authorities

### Tariq Zubair Khan v. Mst. Tabassum Khan — 2024 SCMR 1218
- **Court**: Supreme Court of Pakistan
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority
- **Relevant facts**: Application under Order XXI Rule 90 CPC regarding validity of auction proceedings and objections to the auction sale.
- **The judgment record indicates**: The Supreme Court examined the scope and application of Order XXI Rule 90 CPC. The court addressed limitations on objections to auction proceedings, noting that certain pleas regarding payment of purchase money must be examined within the statutory framework of Order XXI.
- **Ratio decidendi**: The court recognised that applications under Order XXI Rule 90 CPC must be considered within the strict limits of that rule; however, the judgment record does not extract an express limitation period.

### Qazi Humayun v. Mst. Sabiha Qayum — 2023 SCMR 1660
- **Court**: Supreme Court of Pakistan
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority
- **Relevant facts**: Objection petition regarding fraud in the passing of the decree and the sale carried out thereunder; execution of decree in favour of Bank; auction proceedings.
- **The judgment record indicates**: The Supreme Court examined an objection petition challenging the auction proceedings on the ground of fraud. The judgment record indicates consideration of the procedural and substantive grounds available under Order XXI Rule 90 CPC.
- **Ratio decidendi**: The court examined the scope of challenges permissible under Order XXI Rule 90 in the context of allegations of fraud in auction proceedings; however, the judgment record does not establish an express statutory limitation period.

### Allah Wasaya v. Member, Board of Revenue — 2006 YLR 2084
- **Court**: High Court
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority
- **Relevant facts**: Application for review of a decree by the Board of Revenue; approval and confirmation of auction.
- **Court held**: The Supreme Court established that under the statutory review provision examined, "the Limitation for filing such an application is 90 days" from the date of the decree or order. The court stated: "From mere perusal of the above provision of law, it is clear that a person (a) who is an aggrieved by a decree or order by the Board is entitled to apply for its review... (f) the Limitation for filing such an application is 90 days."
- **Ratio decidendi**: Where a statutory review provision expressly prescribes a limitation period, that period (in that case 90 days) is binding and must be strictly observed. However, this decision addresses a specific Board review provision, not Order XXI Rule 90 CPC directly.

### Government of N.-W.F.P. v. Ahmad Shah — 2007 YLR 1781
- **Court**: Peshawar High Court
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority
- **Relevant facts**: Revision petition under Section 115 CPC; judicial consideration of limitation periods prescribed by law for various civil proceedings.
- **Court held**: The court held that "section 115, C.P.C. shall be made within 90 days of the decision of the subordinate Court. Prior to the above-amendment, no statutory period was prescribed by the law for filing of the 'revisions but the superior Courts had always insisted that ordinarily such proceeding should be instituted within the period of 90 days." The court further observed that the Limitation Act contains in its fold remedial provisions like sections 5, 12 and 14, which empowers the Courts to enlarge the period of limitation in peculiar circumstances of each case, provided these provisions have been specifically made applicable on the proceedings.
- **Ratio decidendi**: (A) Statutory revision periods under Section 115 CPC are strictly prescribed; (B) Where no express limitation period is prescribed in the CPC for a specific proceeding, courts do not apply Limitation Act provisions by their own motion unless those provisions are expressly made applicable to that proceeding; (C) General principles of limitation may inform judicial practice, but absence of express statutory limitation does not permit broad judicial extension through remedial provisions of the Limitation Act.

---

## Application to Query

**No express statutory limitation period is prescribed in Order XXI Rule 90 CPC itself.** The bare-act text of Order XXI Rule 90 (1) does not contain a time limit within which an application to set aside an auction sale must be filed. The rule addresses the grounds (material irregularity or fraud), the test of substantial injury, and the deposit/security requirement—but not temporal limitations.

The retrieved Supreme Court authorities do not establish a judicially-created uniform limitation period for Order XXI Rule 90 applications. The principle extracted from *2007 YLR 1781* indicates that where the CPC does not expressly prescribe a limitation period for a proceeding, courts do not independently apply the Limitation Act provisions by their own motion unless those provisions are explicitly made applicable to that proceeding.

**An inference from the cited authorities is** that applications under Order XXI Rule 90 are likely governed by general principles of limitation (such as Article 144 of the Limitation Act 1908, which prescribes 12 years for suits involving immoveable property), or by principles of laches and acquiescence in equity, rather than by a fixed statutory period within Order XXI itself. However, the precise limitation period applicable to such applications would depend on the specific statutory provision invoked (if any) by the court, or on the application of general limitation doctrine to the facts of each case.

**No single Supreme Court judgment in the retrieved authorities squarely holds that Order XXI Rule 90 applications are subject to a specific fixed limitation period (e.g., 30 days, 90 days, or 12 years).** The decision in *2006 YLR 2084* addressed a 90-day limitation under a specific Board review statute, not Order XXI Rule 90. The decision in *2007 YLR 1781* addressed Section 115 CPC revision petitions, which do prescribe a 90-day limitation, but noted the distinction between express and implied limitation periods.

title: Unregistered Tenancy Eviction under PRPA 2009
query: Can an unregistered tenancy agreement be used to evict a tenant under Punjab Rented Premises Act 2009 in Lahore?
memo:
# Legal Memorandum: Unregistered Tenancy Agreement & Eviction Under Punjab Rented Premises Act 2009

## Legal Issue

Whether an unregistered tenancy agreement can be used as evidence to support eviction proceedings under the Punjab Rented Premises Act 2009 in Lahore, and what effect the absence of registration has on the validity and admissibility of such an agreement in Rent Tribunal proceedings.

---

## Relevant Provisions

> Statutory text unavailable in retrieved sources. The analysis is based only on judicial references.

- **Punjab Rented Premises Act, 2009 — Section 5(3)**: Registrar's obligation to enter tenancy particulars in a register and affix official seal on the tenancy agreement.
- **Punjab Rented Premises Act, 2009 — Section 8**: Time limit for initiation of eviction proceedings.
- **Punjab Rented Premises Act, 2009 — Section 9**: Procedural requirements for eviction petitions.
- **Punjab Rented Premises Act, 2009 — Section 15**: Grounds for eviction (expiry of tenancy, default in rent, subletting, breach of agreement, misuse, destruction).
- **Punjab Rented Premises Act, 2009 — Section 34**: Provisions of Qanun-e-Shahadat Order and Code of Civil Procedure do not apply to proceedings under the Act.

---

## Judicial Authorities

### Phipsons Company (Pvt.) Limited v. Zahid Moyeen — PLD 2026 Lahore 172

- **Court**: Lahore High Court
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority (Same statutory framework; same province and forum)
- **Relevant facts**: Eviction petition where the issue of registration of the tenancy agreement under Section 5(3) PRPA 2009 was before the court.
- **Court held**: Though under Section 5(3) of the Punjab Rented Premises Act, 2009, the Rent Registrar is required to enter the particulars of the tenancy in a register and affix his official seal on the tenancy agreement, the scope of this provision—specifically whether failure to register renders the agreement wholly inadmissible or affects its probative value in eviction proceedings—remains a matter of statutory construction and judicial interpretation within the framework of Section 34 PRPA (which displaces ordinary evidence rules).
- **Ratio decidendi**: Registration requirements under Section 5(3) PRPA 2009 impose a procedural obligation on the Rent Registrar, but the judgment indicates that registration and its legal consequences are subject to careful statutory construction. The absence of a complete statutory text precludes definitive statement on whether non-registration is a bar to admissibility or merely affects weight.

---

### Mirza Book Agency v. Additional District Judge, Lahore — 2013 SCMR 1520

- **Court**: Supreme Court of Pakistan
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority (Same statutory framework; Supreme Court precedent)
- **Relevant facts**: Eviction petition under Sections 8, 9, and 15 of the Punjab Rented Premises Act 2009; issues concerning the mandatory time limit for filing and the grounds for eviction.
- **The judgment record indicates**: The Supreme Court considered the 2-year time limit stipulated under Section 8 of the PRPA 2009 as a critical procedural requirement in eviction petitions. The judgment addressed the interplay between the mandatory time-bar and the statutory grounds for eviction under Section 15.
- **Ratio decidendi**: Procedural compliance—including timely filing within Section 8's time limit—is mandatory in eviction proceedings under PRPA 2009. The judgment does not directly address whether an unregistered agreement bars eviction, but establishes that eviction petitions are subject to strict statutory procedures and time limits under PRPA 2009.

---

### Malik Abdul Aziz Awan v. Rana Maqbool Ahmad Khan — 2012 SCMR 91

- **Court**: Supreme Court of Pakistan
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority (Same statutory framework; Supreme Court precedent)
- **Relevant facts**: Ejectment petition involving default in payment of rent under Section 15 and Sections 5-A and 21 of PRPA 2009.
- **The judgment record indicates**: The Supreme Court examined the grounds for eviction under Section 15 (specifically default in payment of rent increase) and considered the interplay with procedural requirements under Section 21 of PRPA 2009. The judgment engaged with the statutory text of Section 15 to determine whether the alleged default constituted a valid ground for eviction.
- **Ratio decidendi**: Eviction proceedings under PRPA 2009 require proof of one or more of the statutory grounds listed in Section 15. The Court's analysis treated Section 15 grounds as exhaustive and mandatory; however, the judgment does not directly address whether an unregistered agreement can establish any of these grounds.

---

### Hassaan Ahmed v. Civil Judge/Special Judge (Rent), Lahore — PLD 2020 Lahore 713

- **Court**: Lahore High Court
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority (Same statutory framework; same province and forum)
- **Relevant facts**: Application for restoration of utility services by a tenant; defect in the tenancy agreement; deposit of fine under Sections 12, 8, and 9 of PRPA 2009.
- **The judgment record indicates**: The Lahore High Court examined the consequences of defects in the tenancy agreement and considered the scope of Section 12 PRPA 2009 in the context of tenancy validity and tenant rights. The judgment engaged with how procedural defects or omissions in the tenancy framework affect substantive outcomes.
- **Ratio decidendi**: Defects or irregularities in the tenancy agreement may have consequences for certain rights and remedies under PRPA 2009, but the judgment does not squarely hold whether non-registration of the agreement bars eviction proceedings.

---

### Abdul Malik Alias Badshah Khan v. Additional District Judge — PLD 2023 Lahore 225

- **Court**: Lahore High Court
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority (Same statutory framework; same province and forum)
- **Relevant facts**: Constitutional petition raising issues of title and ownership determination under Sections 19 and 22 of PRPA 2009; jurisdiction of the Rent Tribunal.
- **The judgment record indicates**: The Lahore High Court considered the scope of determination powers available to the Rent Tribunal under Sections 19 and 22 PRPA 2009, addressing whether the Tribunal may adjudicate disputes beyond eviction to include title determination.
- **Ratio decidendi**: The Rent Tribunal's jurisdiction under PRPA 2009 is confined to eviction and related tenancy disputes; questions of title ownership and ultimate property rights fall outside the Tribunal's domain and may require civil court adjudication in a separate forum (subject to the general exclusion in Section 34 PRPA).

---

**On the admissibility and probative value of an unregistered tenancy agreement in eviction proceedings under PRPA 2009:**

title: PPC Section 406 Criminal Breach of Trust & s.498 CrPC Bail
query: What are the essential ingredients of criminal breach of trust under Section 406 PPC, whether a commercial transaction or loan default constitutes an offence under Section 406 PPC, and what are the governing superior court principles for grant of pre-arrest bail under Section 498 CrPC?
memo:
# LEGAL MEMORANDUM: CRIMINAL BREACH OF TRUST & PRE-ARREST BAIL

## Legal Issue

What are the essential ingredients of criminal breach of trust under Section 406 PPC; whether a commercial transaction or loan default constitutes an offence under Section 406 PPC; and what are the governing superior court principles for grant of pre-arrest bail under Section 498 CrPC?

---

## Relevant Provisions

### Section 405, Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 — Criminal Breach of Trust (Definition)

"Whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property, or with any dominion over property, dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use that property, or dishonestly uses or disposes of that property in violation of any direction of law prescribing the mode in which such trust is to be discharged, or of any legal contract, express or implied, which he has made touching the discharge of such trust, or wilfully suffers any other person so to do, commits 'criminal breach of trust'."

### Section 406, Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 — Punishment for Criminal Breach of Trust

"Whoever commits criminal breach of trust shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both."

**Classification**: Under Cr.P.C. Schedule II, this is a non-bailable, cognizable offence. Compoundable with permission under Section 345(2) Cr.P.C.

### Section 497, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 — When Bail May Be Taken in Non-Bailable Offence

"(1) When any person accused of any non-bailable offence is arrested or detained without warrant by an officer in charge of a police-station, or appears or is brought before a Court, he may be released on bail, but he shall not be so released if there appear reasonable grounds for believing that he has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life or imprisonment for ten years: Provided that the Court may direct that any person under the age of sixteen years or any woman or any sick or infirm person accused of such an offence be released on bail. (2) If it appears to such officer or Court at any stage of the investigation, inquiry or trial, as the case may be, that there are not reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed a non-bailable offence, but that there are sufficient grounds for further inquiry into his guilt, the accused shall, pending such inquiry, be released on bail, or, at the discretion of such officer or Court, on the execution by him of a bond without sureties for his appearance as hereinafter provided."

### Section 498, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 — Power to Direct Admission to Bail or Reduction of Bail

"The amount of every bond executed under this Chapter shall be fixed with due regard to the circumstances of the case, and shall not be excessive; and the High Court or Court of Session may, in any case, whether there be an appeal on conviction or not, direct that any person be admitted to bail, or that the bail required by a police-officer or Magistrate be reduced."

---

## Judicial Authorities

### ISRAR-UL-HAQ v. THE STATE — 2006 YLR 1305

- **Court**: Lahore High Court
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority (Same statutory framework; High Court interpreting Sections 406 PPC and 498 CrPC in bail context)
- **Relevant facts**: Petition for confirmation of ad interim pre-arrest bail in a matter alleged to involve criminal breach of trust and criminal intimidation. The dispute related to business dealings.
- **The judgment record indicates**: That where a matter is essentially of a civil nature and relates to business dealings or contractual disputes, ad interim pre-arrest bail may be confirmed even under Sections 406 and 506 PPC.
- **Ratio decidendi**: The characterization of the underlying dispute (civil vs. criminal) is material to pre-arrest bail consideration. Where the facts disclose a genuine civil commercial dispute rather than a dishonest misappropriation, the granting of pre-arrest bail reflects judicial recognition that Section 406 PPC does not extend to mere contractual defaults or commercial disagreements.

### MUHAMMAD ASHRAF v. STATE — 2006 YLR 2461

- **Court**: Lahore High Court
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority (Same statutory framework; High Court interpreting Sections 406 PPC and 498 CrPC in bail context)
- **Relevant facts**: Pre-arrest bail petition under Section 498 CrPC in a criminal breach of trust case. Investigation was incomplete because recovery was yet to be effected.
- **The judgment record indicates**: Refusal of pre-arrest bail was justified when investigation remained incomplete and recovery remained pending, demonstrating that the stage and state of investigation are material to bail determination.
- **Ratio decidendi**: The completeness of investigation, particularly the recovery of allegedly misappropriated property, is a material consideration in determining whether pre-arrest bail should be granted in Section 406 cases. Incomplete investigation may justify refusal of pre-arrest bail.

### HAKEEM v. STATE — 2026 SCMR 792

- **Court**: Supreme Court of Pakistan
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority (Same statutory framework; Supreme Court interpreting Sections 406, 420, 489-F PPC and Section 497 CrPC)
- **Relevant facts**: Petitioner allegedly involved in agreements with various persons; offences included cheating (Section 420), criminal breach of trust (Section 406), and dishonest issuance of cheque (Section 489-F) under common intention. Co-accused entered into agreements with various persons. Whether offences to the extent of the petitioner required further probe. Investigation had been concluded to the extent of the petitioner.
- **Court held**: 
  - Section 406 PPC offences fall within the non-prohibitory clause of Section 497 CrPC (i.e., bail is the rule and refusal the exception).
  - "While considering the grant of bail, where offences fell within the non-prohibitory clause, the grant of bail had to be considered favourably as a rule, and might be declined in exceptional cases."
  - Exceptional circumstances justifying refusal of bail include: (i) likelihood of abscondence of the accused; (ii) apprehension of the accused tampering with prosecution evidence; (iii) danger of the offence being repeated.
  - Where investigation has been concluded to the extent of the petitioner, further incarceration does not serve a useful purpose, and bail should be granted even in a Section 406 case.
  - Whether the alleged offences were attracted to the petitioner requires further probe; hence a case of "further inquiry" is made out.
- **Ratio decidendi**: Section 406 PPC offences are non-prohibitory bail offences. Grant of bail is the presumptive rule. Refusal is justified only in exceptional cases where there is likelihood of abscondence, evidence tampering, or repetition of offence. The stage of investigation and whether a case requires further inquiry are material factors. A completed or substantially concluded investigation favours grant of bail.

### PLD 2025 SC 866 — ZAHID KHAN v. THE STATE through Prosecutor General, Punjab

- **Court**: Supreme Court of Pakistan
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority (Same statutory framework; Supreme Court interpreting pre-arrest bail practice under Section 498 CrPC)
- **Relevant facts**: Petitioner sought pre-arrest bail before the Supreme Court after the Lahore High Court dismissed his pre-arrest bail petition. Police were treating the mere filing of a petition before the Supreme Court as an implied stay or bar to arrest, despite the High Court's dismissal of pre-arrest bail.
- **Court held**: 
  - "Any practice whereby police authorities treat mere filing of a petition before Supreme Court as an implied stay or bar to arrest, despite dismissal of pre-arrest bail, indicates a misunderstanding of the purpose of pre-arrest bail."
  - Pre-arrest bail exists as "an exceptional measure to protect individuals against arbitrary or mala fide arrest, where circumstances clearly warrant such protection."
  - "Once a competent Court has declined pre-arrest bail, it has necessarily determined that no such exceptional circumstances exist and arrest is lawful and necessary to ensure an effective investigation."
  - Allowing the mere act of filing another petition to operate as a de facto stay would render judicial determination meaningless and defeat the objective of ensuring prompt and fair investigation.
- **Ratio decidendi**: Pre-arrest bail is an exceptional remedy justified only where arbitrary or mala fide arrest is reasonably apprehended. Dismissal of pre-arrest bail by a competent court means no exceptional circumstances exist. Subsequent filing of a petition before a higher court does not suspend the validity of arrest or operate as an implied stay. The finality of judicial determination on pre-arrest bail is critical to investigative integrity.

### Mst. YASMEEN v. STATE — 2006 YLR 2957

- **Court**: Lahore High Court
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority (Same statutory framework; High Court interpreting Section 498 CrPC in pre-arrest bail context)
- **Relevant facts**: Ad interim pre-arrest bail was granted and subsequently confirmed. The grant was made in circumstances where mala fide intention and ulterior motive of the complainant were evident.
- **Court held**: "Bail before arrest is meant to protect innocent citizen if they are found to have been involved in criminal cases with mala fide intention and ulterior motive" (of the complainant).
- **The judgment record indicates**: Pre-arrest bail serves to protect individuals from prosecution motivated by mala fide intent or ulterior motive of the complainant; such circumstance is grounds for confirmation of ad interim pre-arrest bail.
- **Ratio decidendi**: Evidence of mala fide intention or ulterior motive on the part of the complainant is a ground for granting pre-arrest bail, reflecting the protective purpose of Section 498 CrPC against malicious or false prosecution.

---

## Application to Query

### 1. Essential Ingredients of Criminal Breach of Trust under Section 406 PPC

The essential ingredients of criminal breach of trust are established by Section 405 PPC (the definitional provision):

1. **Entrustment of property or dominion over property** — The person must be entrusted with property or have dominion over property in some manner.

2. **Dishonest misappropriation or conversion** — The person must dishonestly misappropriate the property or convert it to their own use, or dishonestly use or dispose of it.

3. **Violation of trust** — This occurs by:
   - Violating any direction of law prescribing the mode in which such trust is to be discharged, OR
   - Violating any legal contract (express or implied) which the person has made touching the discharge of such trust, OR
   - Wilfully suffering any other person to so misappropriate or convert the property.

The essential element is **dishonesty** coupled with a breach of the trust reposed. The trust must arise from an entrustment relation recognized by law or contract.

### 2. Whether Commercial Transaction or Loan Default Constitutes Section 406 Offence

The retrieved authorities establish a critical distinction:

**Commercial Transactions**: In **ISRAR-UL-HAQ v. STATE (2006 YLR 1305)**, the Lahore High Court held that where a matter is "essentially of a civil nature as same related to business," pre-arrest bail may be confirmed even where Sections 406 and 506 PPC are cited. This indicates that **mere commercial disputes, contractual disagreements, or business dealings do not by themselves constitute criminal breach of trust**, even if framed under Section 406. The court's willingness to grant bail in such circumstances reflects the principle that Section 406 PPC does not extend to civil commercial defaults.

**Loan Defaults**: The retrieved authorities do not expressly address whether a loan default (e.g., failure to repay a loan) constitutes criminal breach of trust under Section 406. However, **an inference from the cited authorities is** that a simple loan default (where the borrower received the loan as consideration for a contractual obligation to repay) does not ordinarily attract Section 406 PPC, unless:
- The funds were received not as a loan but under an explicit trust relation (e.g., money given for a specific purpose, held in fiduciary capacity), AND
- The recipient dishonestly misappropriated or diverted those funds in violation of the trust.

If the transaction is genuinely a loan where the borrower obtained full ownership and discretion to use the funds with only an obligation to repay (a debt relation), it remains a civil matter recoverable through ordinary contractual proceedings, not Section 406 PPC.

The distinction is: **A breach of contract to repay a loan ≠ Criminal breach of trust, unless the money was entrusted in a fiduciary or trust capacity and dishonestly misappropriated.**

### 3. Governing Superior Court Principles for Grant of Pre-Arrest Bail under Section 498 CrPC

The Supreme Court and High Court have established the following governing principles:

#### (a) **Section 406 PPC Offences Fall Within Non-Prohibitory Bail Clause**

In **HAKEEM v. STATE (2026 SCMR 792)**, the Supreme Court held that Section 406 PPC offences fall within the non-prohibitory clause of Section 497 CrPC. This means:
- **Grant of bail is the rule; refusal is the exception.**
- Bail must be considered favourably as a starting position.

#### (b) **Exceptional Circumstances Justifying Refusal**

The Supreme Court identified three categories of exceptional circumstances that may justify denial of pre-arrest bail or post-arrest bail in Section 406 cases:

1. **Likelihood of abscondence** — The accused poses a flight risk.
2. **Apprehension of evidence tampering** — The accused is likely to tamper with prosecution evidence, intimidate witnesses, or interfere with the investigation.
3. **Danger of offence repetition** — The nature and circumstances suggest the offence may be repeated.

#### (c) **Stage of Investigation is Material**

In **MUHAMMAD ASHRAF v. STATE (2006 YLR 2461)**, the court recognized that incompleteness of investigation (particularly pending recovery of allegedly misappropriated property) may justify refusal of pre-arrest bail. Conversely, in **HAKEEM (2026 SCMR 792)**, the Court held that where investigation has been substantially concluded to the extent of the petitioner, "his further incarceration would not serve any useful purpose" and bail should be granted.

An inference from these authorities is that courts examine whether further custody is necessary for investigative purposes.

#### (d) **Mala Fide Intention of Complainant is Grounds for Bail**

In **Mst. YASMEEN v. STATE (2006 YLR 2957)**, the court confirmed pre-arrest bail where evidence showed mala fide intention or ulterior motive of the complainant. This reflects the protective purpose of pre-arrest bail: to shield individuals from malicious prosecution.

#### (e) **Pre-Arrest Bail is an Exceptional Remedy**

In **PLD 2025 SC 866 (ZAHID KHAN v. STATE)**, the Supreme Court clarified that pre-arrest bail exists as "an exceptional measure to protect individuals against arbitrary or mala fide arrest, where circumstances clearly warrant such protection." It is not a routine entitlement. Circumstances must demonstrate:
- Genuine apprehension of arbitrary or mala fide arrest, OR
- Exceptional factors warranting protection before arrest.

#### (f) **Finality of Judicial Determination**

In **ZAHID KHAN (PLD 2025 SC 866)**, the Court held that once a competent court has declined pre-arrest bail, it has necessarily determined that no exceptional circumstances exist and arrest is lawful and necessary. Subsequent filing of petitions before a higher court does not operate as a de facto stay. The judicial determination must be respected to preserve investigative integrity.

#### (g) **Discretion of High Court and Court of Session**

Under Section 498 CrPC, the High Court or Court of Session has discretion to direct admission to bail or reduction of bail "in any case," taking due regard to the circumstances of the case and ensuring the bond amount is not excessive.

---

title: Specific Relief Act 1877 Specific Performance & Readiness/Willingness
query: What are the essential conditions for obtaining a decree for specific performance of a contract for sale of immovable property under the Specific Relief Act, 1877, and what is the doctrine of readiness and willingness to perform in Pakistan?
memo:
# LEGAL MEMORANDUM: ESSENTIAL CONDITIONS FOR SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE OF CONTRACTS FOR SALE OF IMMOVABLE PROPERTY & DOCTRINE OF READINESS AND WILLINGNESS

## Legal Issue

What are the essential conditions for obtaining a decree for specific performance of a contract for sale of immovable property under the Specific Relief Act, 1877, and what does the doctrine of readiness and willingness to perform entail in Pakistani law?

---

## Relevant Provisions

### **Specific Relief Act, 1877**

- **Section 12 (Cases in which specific performance enforceable)**: The Court may in its discretion enforce specific performance when: (a) the act is performed as a trust; (b) no standard exists for assessing actual damage from non-performance; (c) pecuniary compensation would not afford adequate relief; or (d) pecuniary compensation cannot be obtained. The Section includes an **Explanation** that presumes breach of a contract to transfer immovable property cannot be adequately relieved by monetary compensation unless proven otherwise.

- **Section 22 (Discretion as to decreeing specific performance)**: The Court's jurisdiction to decree specific performance is discretionary and not arbitrary. The Court is not bound to grant relief merely because it is lawful to do so. The Court may properly exercise discretion *not* to decree specific performance where: (I) circumstances give the plaintiff an unfair advantage over the defendant (absent fraud/misrepresentation); or (II) performance would impose hardship on the defendant unforeseen at contracting, whereas non-performance imposes no such hardship on the plaintiff.

- **Section 24 (Personal bars to the relief)**: Specific performance cannot be enforced in favour of a person who:
  - (a) could not recover compensation for breach;
  - **(b) has become incapable of performing, or violates, any essential term of the contract that on his part remains to be performed** [**doctrine of readiness and willingness**];
  - (c) has already chosen his remedy and obtained satisfaction for the breach;
  - (d) had prior notice that a settlement of the subject-matter had been made and was then in force.

- **Section 27 (Relief against parties claiming under subsequent title)**: Specific performance may be enforced against: (a) either party to the contract; (b) any person claiming under him by subsequent title, **except a transferee for value who has paid his money in good faith and without notice of the original contract** [bona fide purchaser for value without notice]; (c) any person claiming under prior title known to plaintiff but which might have been displaced by defendant.

### **Limitation Act, 1908**

- **Article 113 (For specific performance of a contract)**: The period of limitation is **three years**, running from the date fixed for performance, or if no date is fixed, from when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused.

---

## Judicial Authorities

### **Precedent #1: Liaquat Ali Khan v. Muhammad Akram — 2024 SCMR 1883**
- **Court**: Supreme Court of Pakistan
- **Authority Level**: Analogical Authority (Statutory principle under Section 22, Specific Relief Act; applicable to equitable remedies generally)
- **Relevant facts**: Not fully detailed in the headnote; decision addresses the discretionary nature of specific performance.
- **The judgment record indicates**: Remedy by way of specific performance is equitable and it is not obligatory on the Court to grant such relief merely because it is lawful to do so. Section 22 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 expressly provides that the Court's discretion is not arbitrary but sound and reasonable, guided by judicial principles and capable of correction by a Court of appeal.
- **Ratio decidendi**: The Court's discretion to grant specific performance, whilst not arbitrary, is fundamentally discretionary. The mere lawfulness of specific performance does not mandate its grant; the Court must apply sound judicial principles in determining whether to exercise discretion in favour of the plaintiff.

---

### **Precedent #2: Muhammad Imran v. Ishfaq Ahmed — 2026 SCMR 1063**
- **Court**: Supreme Court of Pakistan
- **Authority Level**: Analogical Authority (Statutory provisions under Section 12 & 39, Specific Relief Act; concerns agreement to sell)
- **Relevant facts**: Not fully detailed; the decision addresses specific performance in the context of non-payment of balance sale consideration and time as essence of contract.
- **The judgment record indicates**: Section 12 & 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 govern specific performance of agreement to sell. The doctrine of time as essence of contract is material when assessing whether a party remains ready and willing to perform.
- **Ratio decidendi**: In contracts for sale of immovable property, readiness and willingness to perform (and compliance with stipulated time) are factors material to the Court's discretionary assessment under Section 12.

---

### **Precedent #3: Faqir Syed Anwar ud Din v. Syed Raza Haider — PLD 2025 SC 31**
- **Court**: Supreme Court of Pakistan
- **Authority Level**: Analogical Authority (Section 27(b), Specific Relief Act; bona fide purchaser for value without notice doctrine)
- **Relevant facts**: Dispute concerning bona fide purchaser status and subsequent title in immovable property.
- **Court held**: In cases involving protection under Section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, the subsequent vendee who asserts bona fide purchaser status must discharge the initial onus. The purchaser must demonstrate: (i) acquisition for due consideration (transferee for value); (ii) a price paid to the vendor (not otherwise); (iii) absence of dishonesty or tainted intention; (iv) that the sale was in good faith (bonafidely); and (v) that reasonable care was exercised in making inquiries expected of a person of ordinary prudence purchasing to acquire good title.
- **Ratio decidendi**: The bona fide purchaser for value exception in Section 27(b) shifts the burden to the subsequent purchaser to affirmatively prove value, legality, good faith, and reasonable diligence. Failure to discharge this burden leaves the purchaser vulnerable to relief sought under specific performance against the original contract.

---

### **Precedent #4: Javed Iqbal v. Mst. Farhat Iqbal (deceased) — 2026 SCMR 1119**
- **Court**: Supreme Court of Pakistan
- **Authority Level**: Analogical Authority (Contract Act ss.211, 214, 215; Specific Relief Act s.39; authority and consent issues in property transfer)
- **Relevant facts**: Dispute concerning validity of property transfer by attorney in favour of attorney's own sons; question of absence of express authority and lack of informed consent of principal.
- **Court held**: In the absence of clear express authority and proven informed consent of the principal, the attorney cannot validly transfer the principal's property in favour of close relatives. Mere production of payment (cheque) by one family member to another does not constitute conclusive proof of a valid sale transaction, particularly absent an agreement to sell or other independent corroborative evidence reflecting a lawful bargain. The legal standard required to validate alienation of immovable property cannot be met by payment evidence alone without establishing the underlying lawful transaction.
- **Ratio decidendi**: For specific performance of a contract for sale of immovable property to succeed, there must exist a valid, lawful underlying agreement. Agreements procured through abuse of fiduciary authority or in the absence of informed consent are not enforceable. Payment alone does not prove the existence of a binding contract or consent to the transaction.

---

title: Limitation on Promissory Note under Limitation Act 1908 & NI Act 1881
query: What is the limitation period for instituting a suit for recovery of money based on a promissory note under the Limitation Act, 1908 and the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 in Pakistan?
memo:
## Legal Issue

What is the limitation period for instituting a suit for recovery of money based on a promissory note under the Limitation Act, 1908 and the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 in Pakistan?

## Relevant Provisions

- **Limitation Act, 1908 — Article 73**: "On a bill of exchange or promissory note payable on demand and not accompanied by any writing restraining or postponing the right to sue. Period of limitation: Three years. Time from which period begins to run: The date of the bill or note."

- **Limitation Act, 1908 — Article 80**: "Suit on a bill of exchange, promissory note or bond not herein expressly provided for. Period of limitation: Three years. Time from which period begins to run: When the bill, note or bond becomes payable."

- **Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 — Section 19**: "A promissory note or bill of exchange is payable on demand,--- (a) where it is expressed to be so, or to be payable at sight or on presentment; or (b) where no time for payment is specified in it; or (c) where the note or bill accepted or indorsed after it is overdue, as regards the person accepting or indorsing it."

## Judicial Authorities

### Taseer Khan v. Islamabad Electricity Supply Company (IESCO) — 2016 YLR 1679

- **Court**: High Court
- **Authority Level**: Direct Authority
- **Relevant facts**: Suit for recovery of amounts; application of limitation periods under Articles 49 & 149, Limitation Act 1908, and Section 79 CPC.
- **The judgment record indicates**: The Supreme Court considered the application of limitation periods in suits for recovery of amounts, recognizing the distinction between limitation periods for suits by private persons and suits by or on behalf of Government.
- **Ratio decidendi**: Courts must apply the appropriate limitation period prescribed under the First Schedule of the Limitation Act, 1908 to suits for recovery, depending on the nature of the instrument and the character of the plaintiff (private or Government).

### Syed Tajuddin v. Afzal Habib — 2006 YLR 537

- **Court**: High Court of Sindh
- **Authority Level**: Analogical Authority (decided under Sindh Rented Premises Ordinance 1979; demonstrates procedural framework for negotiable instruments)
- **Relevant facts**: Suit for recovery of amount on the basis of promissory note; consideration of Negotiable Instruments Act (XXVI of 1861), Section 4; defects in stamping and admissibility of promissory note as evidence.
- **The judgment record indicates**: The Court examined the procedural requirements for suits on promissory notes, including evidentiary standards and the necessity of proper stamping under the Stamp Act.
- **Ratio decidendi**: A promissory note must satisfy evidential and statutory requirements (including proper stamping) to form a valid basis for a suit for recovery; procedural defects can render the instrument inadmissible even if the underlying cause of action exists.

### First Islamic Modaraba v. Dawood Capital Management Limited — 2026 CLD 731

- **Court**: High Court of Sindh
- **Authority Level**: Analogical Authority (decided under Companies Ordinance 1984; illustrates application of limitation principles to financial obligations)
- **Relevant facts**: Delayed recovery action on unpaid Musharika finance facility of Rs. 20 million extended in 2005; legal notice issued in 2010; winding-up petition filed over five years after cause of action arose.
- **The judgment record indicates**: The Court held that when the time for recovery of a debt itself becomes time-barred, any notice issued subsequent to the expiry of the limitation period is of no effect.
- **Ratio decidendi**: Issuance of a statutory notice after the limitation period has expired cannot extend or revive the right to sue; the limitation period remains absolute in its operation once the period prescribed under the Limitation Act has passed.

## Application to Query

Under Pakistani law, the limitation period for instituting a suit for recovery of money based on a promissory note is governed by **Article 73 or Article 80** of the Limitation Act, 1908, depending on the nature and terms of the promissory note.

**Article 73** prescribes a **three-year limitation period** for suits on a bill of exchange or promissory note **payable on demand** (where no time for payment is specified, or where the note is expressed to be payable at sight or on presentment). The period begins to run **from the date of the bill or note**.

**Article 80** prescribes a **three-year limitation period** for suits on a bill of exchange, promissory note or bond **not expressly provided for** in other articles of the First Schedule. The period begins to run **when the bill, note or bond becomes payable**.

Under **Section 19 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881**, a promissory note is payable on demand where (a) it is expressed to be so, or payable at sight or on presentment; (b) no time for payment is specified; or (c) the note is accepted or indorsed after it is overdue.

The distinction between the two articles depends on whether a specific time for payment is provided in the promissory note. If the promissory note is silent on the time for payment or is explicitly stated to be payable on demand, Article 73 applies. If a time for payment is specified, Article 80 applies, and the limitation period commences when that specified time arrives.

The judicial precedents indicate that once the three-year limitation period expires, a suit cannot be instituted, and any subsequent attempt to recover (including the issuance of legal notices after the period has elapsed) does not revive or extend the right to sue.
